text: One process tells you a program ran. A process tree tells you the entire sequence that led to it running -- every parent-child launch relationship chained together from the creation telemetry we covered last lesson. That's exactly the shape most attacks take: not a single malicious file, but a chain of ordinary-looking steps. Here's how EDR reads that chain, and why the same kind of relationship can be completely harmless or a near-automatic alert.

A parent-child relationship by itself proves nothing -- processes launch other processes constantly. services.exe launching svchost.exe dozens of times at boot is routine. explorer.exe launching whatever a user double-clicks is routine. What makes a specific lineage worth flagging is which two processes are involved: winword.exe launching powershell.exe has no legitimate business reason to happen, because a document editor has no reason to start a scripting engine -- and that pattern alone is close to an automatic red flag.

A tree's value compounds the deeper it goes. winword.exe spawning powershell.exe is already suspicious on its own. Extend it one more hop to winword.exe to powershell.exe to certutil.exe, and the concern grows further -- a built-in Windows utility often abused to download or decode payloads, launched from a chain that started with a document editor. Each additional unexpected hop adds confidence this is a staged sequence, not coincidence.

A user opens an invoice attachment. The resulting tree is outlook.exe to winword.exe to powershell.exe to certutil.exe. Outlook launching Word is completely normal -- opening an attachment does exactly that. The moment the chain extends to Word launching PowerShell, a behavioral rule fires: 'Office application spawned a script interpreter.' The analyst doesn't need to identify the malware family -- the lineage pattern alone is enough to generate a high-confidence alert and, on many platforms, block the child process automatically.

That's the real power of behavioral detection: it flags the shape of a sequence, not a known-bad file. Next, we'll look at why attackers lean so heavily on legitimate, pre-installed tools like PowerShell and certutil in the first place -- living-off-the-land techniques built specifically to blend into lineage a signature scanner would never catch.
